The federal minimum wage should be raised significantly to ensure a living wage for all workers. Currently, the federal minimum of $7.25 per hour is woefully inadequate, failing to keep pace with inflation and leaving millions of full-time workers in poverty. Raising it to at least $15—or higher in high-cost areas—would reduce income inequality, stimulate economic growth by increasing consumer spending, and lift many families out of financial distress. Critics argue that higher wages could lead to job losses, but empirical studies, such as those from the Economic Policy Institute, show that moderate increases have minimal negative employment effects while substantially improving workers' quality of life.  

My support for this policy stems from a belief in economic justice and human dignity. No one working full-time should struggle to afford basic necessities like housing, food, or healthcare. A higher minimum wage also reduces reliance on government assistance programs, effectively shifting the burden from taxpayers to employers who can afford to pay fair wages. While some small businesses may face challenges, phased implementation and targeted support can mitigate disruptions. Ultimately, a significant raise aligns with the principle that prosperity should be broadly shared, not concentrated at the top. The government has a moral obligation to act.
